questions.question: In an R1CS, each constraint has which general form?
options: (linear combination) · (linear combination) = (linear combination)
(quadratic polynomial) = 0
hash(message) = digest
questions.explanation: R1CS constraints multiply two linear combinations and equate them to a third linear combination over a field.

questions.question: Over a field, what does it mean to say that t(x) divides P(x)?
options: There exists a polynomial h(x) such that P(x) = t(x)·h(x) with zero remainder
P(x) and t(x) have the same degree
P(x) and t(x) share at least one root
questions.explanation: Divisibility means exact multiplication in the polynomial ring, i.e. polynomial long division leaves remainder 0.

questions.question: If the constraint domain is {1, 2}, what is the target/vanishing polynomial t(x)?
questions.explanation: By definition t(x)=∏(x-x_i), so for points 1 and 2 it is (x-1)(x-2).

questions.question: If an R1CS has m constraints and you build per-wire polynomials by interpolation on m points, what degree bound do those polynomials have?
options: Degree < m
Degree ≤ m
Degree < m^2
No degree bound; it can be arbitrarily large
questions.explanation: Interpolation on m points produces a unique polynomial of degree at most m-1, i.e. degree < m.

questions.question: Why does QAP define one polynomial per wire (column) rather than one polynomial per constraint (row)?
options: So a witness vector a can form aggregated polynomials A(x)=Σ a_j·A_j(x), B(x), C(x) with a single linear combination
So all polynomials automatically have degree 1
To avoid computing any field inverses
Because Groth16 requires exactly three polynomials total
questions.explanation: The per-wire polynomials let the prover/verifier aggregate using the witness coefficients consistently across A, B, and C.

questions.question: In the QAP check, why does t(x) | (A(x)B(x) - C(x)) capture 'all constraints are satisfied'?
options: Because t(x) vanishes on all constraint points, and divisibility means A(x)B(x)-C(x) vanishes on the same set
Because any divisible polynomial must be constant
Because polynomial division is faster than multiplication
Because t(x) encodes the witness directly
questions.explanation: If a polynomial has all x_i as roots, it must be a multiple of the product ∏(x-x_i), which is t(x).

questions.question: Which choice of constraint points {x_i} makes Lagrange interpolation invalid (or forces division by zero) in a prime field?
options: Two points are equal modulo p
All points are non-zero modulo p
The points are in increasing order
The points are small integers
questions.explanation: Interpolation uses denominators (x_i - x_j); if any x_i == x_j (mod p), a denominator becomes 0.

questions.question: Why isn't the bare statement 't(x) divides A(x)B(x)-C(x)' sufficient by itself to make a secure SNARK verifier?
options: A cheating prover must be forced (cryptographically) to use the correct per-wire polynomials and one consistent witness; otherwise they can fake A,B,C to satisfy the division
Because polynomial divisibility is undefined over fields
Because QAP only works for addition gates, not multiplication gates
Because t(x) must always be irreducible
questions.explanation: SNARKs add commitments/CRS machinery so the prover can't choose arbitrary polynomials; the algebra must be tied to the circuit and witness.
